title: Jetstream pressure probe - cold/warm KV interplay
content:
Objective:
- Understand how sudden request surges (jetstream-like bursts) interact with KV cache warm vs cold state and continuous batching.
- Find quick knobs to reduce p99 tail on mixed workloads without sacrificing steady-state throughput.

Hypotheses before runs:
1) Cold KV cache + high concurrency -> p99 spikes driven by tokenizer + memory touch / kv-pop penalties.
2) Continuous batching reduces per-token cost but can increase p95 for short requests when batch-timeout is too high.
3) Small increase in KV cache size or tweak to eviction policy will drop p99 significantly for bursty traffic.

Environment / baseline:
- Model variant: open-32k-quant-v1 (approx 7B baseline for these runs)
- Hardware: A100-sim cluster (4x A100 nodes behind routing pool), single replica used for isolation runs
- Runtime flags: batching=continuous, batch_timeout_ms=5/20/50 (varied), kv_cache=true, kv_size_limit_mb=4096 (default), eviction_policy=LRU
- Workloads:
  * S1 cold-spike: 2m idle, then 12s high-intensity spike (peak QPS 480), payloads ~100 tokens (avg 1200 seq tokens incl. priming).
  * S2 warm-steady: warm cache (run warmup for 10m), steady QPS 200 for 10m, payload avg 40 tokens.
  * S3 mixed-random: alternating 30s low (QPS 50) / 30s medium (QPS 220) over 20m with Poisson jitter.
- Metrics collected: RPS, p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side), GPU utilization (%), GPU mem usage, KV cache hit rate, batching stats (avg batch size, batch wait latency)

Commands / harness notes:
- k6 load scripts with custom arrival patterns; using our local bench harness: bench/run_agent --profile jetstream-spike --concurrency 200
- curl to control plane: POST /v1/models/open-32k-quant-v1/serve/config {batch_timeout_ms, kv_cache:true}
- logs: /var/log/serving-runtime/jetstream-*.log (grep for kv-evict, batch-emit)

Results summary (selected runs):
- Run A (cold-spike, batch_timeout_ms=20):
  RPS peak: 468
  p50: 28 ms, p95: 210 ms, p99: 1.85 s
  GPU util: 92% (spike sustained ~12s)
  KV hit rate: 12% (cold)
  avg batch size: 6
  notes: multiple 1.6-1.9s tail events coincident with kv-evict log messages and OOM-like slowdowns when node touched previously-unused pages.

- Run B (cold-spike, batch_timeout_ms=5):
  RPS peak: 420 (slightly lower due to reduced batching effectiveness)
  p50: 24 ms, p95: 180 ms, p99: 1.15 s
  GPU util: 88%
  KV hit rate: 10%
  avg batch size: 3
  notes: lower p99 vs Run A. Hypothesis: shorter wait reduces batch-assembly delays during cache misses; fewer requests get stuck waiting behind a long batch when they require expensive cold memory touches.

- Run C (warm-steady, batch_timeout_ms=20):
  RPS: 205 steady
  p50: 22 ms, p95: 75 ms, p99: 150 ms
  GPU util: 70%
  KV hit rate: 86%
  avg batch size: 8
  notes: expected behavior; batching yields good throughput and low tail.

- Run D (mixed-random, batch_timeout_ms=20, kv_size_limit_mb=2048):
  observed intermittent p99 spikes to ~900ms during transition windows when QPS increased. KV hit rate fell from 78% to ~52% at peak, matching an observed burst of cache evictions (eviction logs at same timestamps).

Key observations / anomalies:
- Cold-cache penalty is not purely token-decode compute; many p99 events show large time in "kv-pop" path and page faults when memory touched after idle. This suggests OS-level page-in + allocator fragmentation contributes to the long tail.
- Reducing batch_timeout helps p99 on cold spikes, at cost of RPS. There's a sweet spot for short requests where batch_timeout 5-10ms reduces tail without losing too much throughput.
- Eviction storms (when kv_size_limit lowered) create transient p99s even in warm workloads because evicted keys are frequently re-requested in bursts.
- GPU utilization correlates with throughput but isn’t the tail driver; tails are dominated by host-side cache/mem behavior and batching waits.

Quick actionable next steps (low-effort / high-impact):
1) Short-term: lower default batch_timeout for small-payload endpoints to 8ms via route override for webhook/short-prompt usage. Add a per-route heuristic: if median request tokens < 60 -> batch_timeout 8ms. (Create small flag PR)
2) Increase kv_size_limit_mb for the A100 pool serving customer-facing endpoints that experience bursty traffic; +25% reduces eviction churn in tests.
3) Investigate OS-level swipe-page behavior: schedule a run with hugepages enabled or pre-touch memory on container startup to reduce page-in cost.
4) Add a quick metric: measure "host page fault count" per request and ship in traces to correlate with p99.

Ideas for more in-depth experiments:
- Run with different eviction policies (CLOCK vs LRU) under mixed workload to see if CLOCK prevents eviction storms for hot prefixes.
- Repeat cold spike with different quantization (int8 vs int4) to see if reduced model memory footprint reduces page-in cost and tail.
- Try disabling continuous batching and use micro-batching with adaptive routing to privileged fast-path for small-requests.
- Synthetic microbench: pre-touch memory pages in a warmup process and compare tails.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Are tails happening on specific cores or threads? Need per-thread CPU sampling during cold spikes (perf + flame).
- Does the network stack amplify tail events when combined with page faults? Correlate netstat/tcp-queue depth during events.
- How much of the tail can be moved from server to client by returning partial responses earlier? Explore partial-prefix streaming for heavy-token outputs.

Notes to self / quick log: 
- Diego saw similar eviction pattern on Nov 1; linked his logs in the Confluence page.
- Slack threads: #perf-alerts (see thread starting 2024-11-03 10:12) has raw k6 scripts.
- Leave trace_id prefixes in bench harness for easier join with logs.

Decision suggestions to product/ops (short):
- For customer routes with <100 token medians and history of burstiness, provide a recommended default route config template: {batch_timeout_ms:8, kv_size_limit_mb:+25%, prewarm_on_scale:true}.
- Add a small perf-obs job that runs jetstream-style burst once per day on staging to detect regressions introduced by eviction or batch changes.

Appendix: quick raw table (for copy to ticket)
Scenario | batch_timeout | peak RPS | p95 | p99 | KV hit
Cold-spike (A) | 20ms | 468 | 210ms | 1850ms | 12%
Cold-spike (B) | 5ms  | 420 | 180ms | 1150ms | 10%
Warm-steady (C) | 20ms | 205 | 75ms  | 150ms  | 86%
Mixed (D) | 20ms | 220 | 130ms | 900ms | 52%

End-of-note: leave this doc as working scratch — will iterate after next run where we try hugepages + CLOCK eviction.
